passages.title: Book Review on Musicophilia
passages.subtitle: Norman M. Weinberger reviews the latest work of Oliver Sacks on music.
content: [A]  Music and the brain are both endlessly fascinating subjects, and as a neuroscientist specialising in auditory learning and memory, I find them especially intriguing. So I had high expectations of Musicophilia, the latest offering from neurologist and prolific author Oliver Sacks. And I confess to feeling a little guilty reporting that my reactions to the book are mixed.

[B]  Sacks himself is the best part of Musicophilia. He richly documents his own life in the book and reveals highly personal experiences. The photograph of him on the cover of the book— which shows him wearing headphones, eyes closed, clearly enchanted as he listens to Alfred Brendel perform Beethoven's Pathétique Sonata-makes a positive impression that is borne out by the contents of the book. Sacks' voice throughout is steady and erudite but never pontifical. He is neither self-conscious nor self-promoting.

[C]  The preface gives a good idea of what the book will deliver. In it, Sacks explains that he wants to convey the insights gleaned from the "enormous and rapidly growing body of work on the neural underpinnings of musical perception and imagery, and the complex and often bizarre disorders to which these are prone." He also stresses the importance of "the simple art of observation" and "the richness of the human context." He wants to combine "observation and description with the latest in technology," he says, and to imaginatively enter into the experience of his patients and subjects. The reader can see that Sacks, who has been practicing neurology for 40 years, is torn between the "old-fashioned" path of observation and the new-fangled, high-tech approach: He knows that he needs to take heed of the latter, but his heart lies with the former.

[D]  The book consists mainly of detailed descriptions of cases, most of them involving patients whom Sacks has seen in his practice. Brief discussions of contemporary neuroscientific reports are sprinkled liberally throughout the text. Part I, "Haunted by Music," begins with the strange case of Tony Cicoria, a nonmusical, middle-aged surgeon who was consumed by a love of music after being hit by lightning. He suddenly began to crave listening to piano music, which he had never cared for in the past. He started to play the piano and then to compose music, which arose spontaneously in his mind in a "torrent" of notes. How could this happen? Was the cause psychological? (He had had a near-death experience when the lightning struck him.) Or was it the direct result of a change in the auditory regions of his cerebral cortex? Electroencephalography (EEG) showed his brain waves to be normal in the mid-1990s, just after his trauma and subsequent "conversion" to music. There are now more sensitive tests, but Cicoria has declined to undergo them; he does not want to delve into the causes of his musicality. What a shame!

[E]  Part II, "A Range of Musicality," covers a wider variety of topics, but unfortunately, some of the chapters offer little or nothing that is new. For example, chapter 13, which is five pages long, merely notes that the blind often have better hearing than the sighted. The most interesting chapters are those that present the strangest cases. Chapter 8 is about "amusia," an inability to hear sounds like music, and "dysharmonia," a highly specific impairment of the ability to hear harmony, with the ability to understand melody left intact. Such specific "dissociations" are found throughout the cases Sacks recounts.

[F]  To Sacks's credit, part III, "Memory, Movement and Music," brings us into the underappreciated realm of music therapy. Chapter 16 explains how "melodic intonation therapy" is being used to help expressive aphasic patients (those unable to express their thoughts verbally following a stroke or other cerebral incident) once again become capable of fluent speech. In chapter 20, Sacks demonstrates the near-miraculous power of music to animate Parkinson's patients and other people with severe movement disorders, even those who are frozen into odd postures. Scientists cannot yet explain how music achieves this effect.

[G]  To readers who are unfamiliar with neuroscience and music behavior, Musicophilia may be something of a revelation. But the book will not satisfy those seeking the causes and implications of the phenomena Sacks describes. For one thing, Sacks appears to be more at ease discussing patients than discussing experiments. And he tends to be rather uncritical in accepting scientific findings and theories.

[H]  It's true that the causes of music-brain oddities remain poorly understood. However, Sacks could have done more to draw out some of the implications of the careful observations that he and other neurologists have made and of the treatments that have been successful. For example, he might have noted that the many specific dissociations among components of music comprehension, such as loss of the ability to perceive harmony but not melody, indicate that there is no music center in the brain. Because many people who read the book are likely to believe in the brain localisation of all mental functions, this was a missed educational opportunity.

[I]  Another conclusion one could draw is that there seem to be no "cures" for neurological problems involving music. A drug can alleviate a symptom in one patient and aggravate it in another or can have both positive and negative effects in the same patient. Treatments mentioned seem to be almost exclusively antiepileptic medications, which "damp down" the excitability of the brain in general; their effectiveness varies widely.

[J]  Finally, in many of the cases described here the patient with music-brain symptoms is reported to have "normal" EEG results. Although Sacks recognises the existence of new technologies, among them far more sensitive ways to analyze brain waves than the standard neurological EEG test, he does not call for their use. In fact, although he exhibits the greatest compassion for patients, he conveys no sense of urgency about the pursuit of new avenues in the diagnosis and treatment of music-brain disorders. This absence echoes the book's preface, in which Sacks expresses fear that "the simple art of observation may be lost" if we rely too much on new technologies. He does call for both approaches, though, and we can only hope that the neurological community will respond.

passages.title: Getting a visa to travel to Thailand
content: 📌 Getting a visa to travel to Thailand
Main types of visa:
- Business visa (for working in Thailand)
lasts for [ _____ ] days
- For people going to Thailand on holiday or visiting for [ _____ ] reasons
lasts for 60 days
Getting a tourist visa
- may need to provide a [ _____ ] certificate or a driving licence
- will need a passport that is still valid for a minimum of [ _____ ]
- need to:
fill in a form to apply for a tourist visaprovide two passport photos - must be [ _____ ] and the same size
📌 Tourist visa application form
PERSONAL DETAILS
Nationality: [ _____ ]Surname: JohnstonFirst name: AlanMiddle name: [ _____ ]Mobile number: [ _____ ]
TRAVEL DETAILS
Years of previous trips to Thailand: 1992 and [ _____ ]Start date of visa for travel to Thailand: September 1Probable destination country after departure from Thailand: [ _____ ]
transcript: [00:46] Alan: Good morning. I'm planning a trip to Thailand soon and I'd like to make a visa application please. There seem to be so many different types.
[00:56] Officer: You're right, there are. But there are two popular, more common ones.
[01:01] Alan: What are the main differences between them?

[01:04] Officer: The business visa lasts for 90 days. This is for people coming to begin work or do business in the country. The other one, which is for people going on holiday or for medical treatment, lasts 60 days. Are you planning on travelling for work or pleasure?
[01:20] Alan: I'm actually going to visit a friend who works over there, so for pleasure. I'll be doing a lot of travelling and sightseeing, I imagine.

[01:29] Officer: OK, so you need the tourist visa. There are several things you need to make the application. Now, depending on your situation, we might have to ask you for additional documents, such as a birth certificate or driving licence, but we do need to see a passport in all cases.
[01:47] Alan: I've got that here with me and I've also taken a copy of it for you. I thought it might be necessary.

[01:53] Officer: Let me see. I'm afraid you will need to apply for a new one. This one runs out in November, which is in five months, and it has to have at least six left on it for the visa application.
[02:06] Alan: Right, I see. OK, I can do that. What else?
[02:11] Officer: You need to complete this tourist visa application form and attach two photographs too. Do you have any passport photos?
[02:19] Alan: No, but when I apply for my new passports, I will get some. Do they need to be the same size?
[02:26] Officer: Exactly the same. They must be recent too, but that won't be a problem if you're getting some done anyway. Next thing is to complete the application form.
[02:35] Alan: OK, let's see. Would you be able to help me complete it?
[03:24] Officer: Of course. Let's have a look. Right, so fill in all your personal information.
[03:30] Alan: Great.
[03:32] Officer: Nationality is British, surname is Johnston and first name is Alan. Can I just confirm your middle name? It's not very clear on the form. Is that Senmore?
[03:45] Officer: S-E-N?
[03:47] Alan: No, sorry, it's my handwriting. It should say Seymour. That's S-E-Y-M-O-U-R.
[03:56] Officer: Thank you. I've got that now. So we also need your mobile number. Could I make a note of it?
[04:22] Officer: Got it. Everything seems to be in order in that section of the form. Let's have a look at the next part, about previous travel to the country.
[04:32] Alan: Yes, do I need to complete that section, or is that only for long-term visas?
[04:38] Officer: No, no, you have to complete it. So the first point asks if you have travelled to Thailand before.
[04:45] Alan: Yes, but it was many years ago, in 1992 and 1990... let me think... 1996. No, wait, that was the year I travelled to Vietnam.
[05:00] Officer: OK. And when are you going to travel to Thailand this time? The date you give me must be no more than three months after the issue date of the visa.
[05:09] Alan: I understand. Well, I'm supposed to be there for my friend's birthday in September.
[05:15] Officer: And when exactly is your friend's birthday?
[05:17] Alan: 15th of September.
[05:19] Officer: Let's put down the first of that month.

[05:21] Alan: Great. And what about this last part on the form, here? It asks about departure from Thailand. My friend and I are talking about going on to Bali after Thailand, but really, I think I'm going to come back home to England.
[05:39] Alan: He might go to Bali alone.
[05:41] Officer: OK, so we can fill that part in. And that's everything. Now come back again with your new passport as soon as you have it, and we can issue your visa.
[05:50] Alan: Thanks a lot for your help.

questions.prompt: lasts for _____ days

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "What are the main differences between them? The business visa lasts for 90 days."
explanation.step3: .. days") ▶️ Thông tin cần nghe ở : đoạn từ 00:01:04, khi Officer bắt đầu giải thích về sự khác nhau giữa các loại visa. ☺️ Cùng xem giải thích nhé : Officer nói rõ rằng "The business visa lasts for 90 days." Nghĩa là visa công tác sẽ có hiệu lực trong 90 ngày. Vì đề hỏi "business visa lasts for ___ days", nên ta điền số 90 . ✅ Đáp án đúng: 90 🧐 Lưu ý bẫy đề thi : ❌ 60 => Đây là thời hạn của tourist visa (visa du lịch), không phải business visa.

questions.prompt: - For people going to Thailand on holiday or visiting for _____ reasons

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "The other one, which is for people going on holiday or for medical treatment, lasts 60 days."
explanation.step3: ☺️ Cùng xem giải thích nhé : Officer nói "The other one, which is for people going on holiday or for medical treatment..." . Ở đây, "medical treatment" chính là lý do khác ngoài đi du lịch. Vì đề bài hỏi "holiday or ____ reasons", ta chọn từ medical để điền, do "medical reasons" là cụm tự nhiên và chính xác trong tiếng Anh. ✅ Đáp án đúng: medical 🧐 Lưu ý bẫy đề thi : ❌ holiday => "Holiday" đã được nhắc đến trước đó trong câu hỏi, không thể điền lại. ❌ work => "Work" liên quan đến business visa , không phải tourist visa .

questions.prompt: - may need to provide a _____ certificate or a driving licence

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "Now, depending on your situation, we might have to ask you for additional documents, such as a birth certificate or driving licence, but we do need to see a passport in all cases."
explanation.step3: ☺️ Cùng xem giải thích nhé : Officer nói "we might have to ask you for additional documents, such as a birth certificate or driving licence" . Từ khóa "birth certificate" trùng khớp hoàn toàn với chỗ trống cần điền. passages.title: Apartment building: Piano tower
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Apartment building: Piano tower"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:43] AUDIO: Good evening everybody. I'm Sarah, the sales manager for the apartments here at Piano Tower, which is itself a fantastic piece of early 20th century architecture. People say it looks like an old warehouse, but it was designed for manufacturing pianos. And this was a great location for that because the railway is close by, so the instruments could be transported by train for sale in shops around the country.

[01:15] AUDIO: When the piano firm closed, the building was occupied for a time by a group who did printmaking, photography and painting here until the building was purchased by us about three years ago and converted into these wonderful apartments. This will be a fabulous place to live, with great facilities for the residents to enjoy full and healthy lifestyles. There's a gym in the building, which residents will have access to at no extra charge. But that's not the only way they'll be keeping fit, because they'll also get a reduction on the price of a swim in the pool.

[01:52] AUDIO: The room we're in now, the common room, is a shared space that residents can use, either for work meetings or for socializing. They won't have to pay for this, but they'll need to book, and it's first come, first serve. Also worthy of mention is that anybody with a vehicle has the option of renting a space in our secure basement car park if they wish, and there'll be a laundry room available for a small charge each time you use it, or you can have unlimited use for a monthly fee. We are very proud of how sustainable Piano Tower is.

[02:30] AUDIO: For example, the roof's covered with grass and wildflowers to encourage birds and insects. The apartments are all energy efficient, with large windows that let in the sun. Some of the apartments on the ground floor are equipped with heat pumps for radiators and hot water, while the others have the latest gas boilers. Obviously the original building was constructed with man-made materials, brick, steel and concrete.

[02:57] AUDIO: But during the conversion, wherever possible, the architects used organic materials that are found in nature. Examples include the wooden floors in the apartments, which are from timber grown sustainably in the area, and the sheep's wall, which was used as insulation in the walls. We actually have over 40 apartments for sale, but please believe me when I tell you that each one is unique in its own way. I'd like to tell you about four of them to show you what I mean.

[04:09] AUDIO: Starting with the Keyboard apartment. Internally, there's one large living and sleeping area. This apartment is competitively priced. The whole apartment is unfurnished, so the buyer will be able to choose whatever kitchen and bathroom they want, and add their own touch to make it their perfect home.

[04:29] AUDIO: And externally, there's a lovely shaded courtyard, which will be a perfect spot for eating outdoors on those summer evenings. For anyone looking for a larger property, we have the Brubeck, a four-bedroom flat on the top floor. Part of this was originally the director's office, and the windows stretch all the way around the apartment, giving you a fabulous 360-degree panorama over the rooftops of the city. As I mentioned, the majority of the apartments are unfurnished.

[05:04] AUDIO: However, our next apartment, Sonata Rooms, is different. It's already got everything you'd need, from a gorgeous fully-fitted kitchen, even with pots and pans, right through to a huge flat-screen TV. It's literally ready to move into. And finally, the Nyman flat, which is on the second floor, in the part of the complex closest to the river, which you can actually see out of every single window in this fantastic three-bedroom flat.

[05:35] AUDIO: So even though you're in the heart of the city, it's a great place to just sit back and watch the wildlife. Anyway, I've got printed brochures with the specifications of each apartment, along with pricing, so if anyone would like to...

passages.title: Work Placement
content: 📌 How to proceed with the reflective portfolio
transcript: [00:53] Sarah: Hi James, this is our first face-to-face tutorial in a while and I just wanted to check in with you after your work placement.
[01:01] James: Okay, it's all been really useful I think.
[01:04] Sarah: And you've been working for a manufacturing company, is that right?
[01:07] James: Yes, they make baby products actually.
[01:10] Sarah: Sounds interesting. Tell me about why you chose to work there.

[01:14] James: Well, actually it was my first choice. Everybody else was applying to the software company and I thought that I might not get it. I didn't really care about the products in the baby company but what interested me the most was that it's a huge multinational company and I thought it would be a really interesting experience working for an organisation like that.
[01:37] Sarah: And do you think you made the right choice?

[01:39] James: Well, yes and no. I mean, probably the best bit of working for a company like that is that there's so much stuff going on in terms of market analysis, which I've always been interested in, but also research and development, product and design and lots of stuff that I've never really thought of before.
[01:59] Sarah: It sounds like it was all good.

[02:01] James: Well, yes, but I also think that if I'd chosen to do my placement with a smaller company, I'd have been able to make more of an impact. I just sometimes felt that the stakes were so high there. Everything involved huge amounts of money and that stopped people taking risks or allowing someone like me to have any real impact on the tasks.
[02:23] Sarah: Yes, that can sometimes be the case. It's useful to get some feedback. Do you think it was well organised?

[02:29] James: Oh, yes, it was great. I had a mentor the whole time who I could ask if I had any problems, so even as I moved around departments and had different managers, I always had the same person to talk to if I had any problems.
[03:24] Sarah: Good. Well, I look forward to reading about it in your reflective portfolio.
[03:30] James: That's what I wanted to talk to you about, actually. I'm not really sure how to go about it.
[03:36] Sarah: Okay, well, I can help you with that. Do you have your notes?
[03:40] James: Yes, here they are. So, what I'm not really sure about is how to structure it.

[03:46] Sarah: Well, what you need to start by doing is looking at the module handbook. This tells you the knowledge and skills that you have to demonstrate. If you take notes on these things, then you will have the content that you need.
[03:59] James: Okay, I'll have a look at that again. That's good to know. But I'm still not sure about the structure. Is it like an essay?

[04:07] Sarah: No, the portfolio has a different structure. I don't really want to tell you exactly how to do it as there are different ways that are good for different people. After organising your notes, you could go to the library and look at the student assignment there from last year. It's in the section near the study skills books.
[04:25] Sarah: It was a really good example and you can get some ideas about layout. I'll email you the details.
[04:32] James: Thanks, that would be great. So, do I need to choose some headings?

[04:37] Sarah: Yes, you can look at the learning objectives for the course to get ideas about that. There's a list of different things which you could discuss in each section. Evidence of problem solving, understanding of organisational structure, evaluation of training and so on.
[04:53] James: Okay, that's kind of clear. So, can I write a draft and then get some feedback from you?
[04:59] Sarah: Well, like all written work, I can only give you feedback on 20% of it. So, I suggest that you write a couple of sections and I'll look at that.
[05:07] James: Thanks, that'll help a lot. Just to let me know if I'm on the right track.

[05:11] Sarah: Also, there's another great place to check suggestions, get feedback and bounce ideas around and that's the online forum. All of your classmates are posting and can answer any questions you have. Getting into a discussion online is a great way to develop your thoughts further.
[05:28] James: Yes, I'd forgotten about that. Thanks, you've given me a lot to get on with.

[05:33] Sarah: Oh, one last thing. Make sure that after you've finished, you get somebody else to proofread it for you. If you do it yourself, then you might miss things. I always recommend that my students swap papers to look for errors and make suggestions.
[05:47] James: Okay, will do. Thanks a lot, Sarah.
[05:50] Sarah: No problem. I look forward to seeing what you come up with.

passages.title: The Chimp Paradox by Professor Steve Peters
content: 📌 The Chimp Paradox by Professor Steve Peters
The basic idea of The Chimp Paradox
Sometimes, humans behave a bit like chimpanzees!
According to Peters, the brain contains two parts: 'human' and 'chimp'
- The 'human' is the part of the brain that:
is usually [ _____ ]likes to have [ _____ ]
- The 'chimp'
is more [ _____ ] than the humancan be a friend or an enemy
Having these two very different parts of the brain often leads to a [ _____ ] ; this is the 'chimp paradox'
Examples of the chimp paradox
entering a room full of [ _____ ] and being unsure how to reactdeciding whether to complete a dull task or to [ _____ ]
Applications of The Chimp Paradox in sport
The Chimp Paradox famously helped convince a well-known [ _____ ] to continue. She says the 'chimp' approach helped her become a [ _____ ]
Snooker player Ronnie O'Sullivan said that Peters' ideas enabled him to deal with [ _____ ] . Peters encouraged O'Sullivan to find time for [ _____ ], which he enjoyed
transcript: [01:06] AUDIO: Hi everyone. So when our teacher asked us to prepare a presentation about how psychology affects sporting success, I immediately knew I wanted to talk about the Chimp Paradox. Now for anyone who doesn't know, the Chimp Paradox is a popular psychology book by Steve Peters and it's been highly influential. It's basically suggesting that people behave a bit like chimpanzees, animals which you might have seen in zoos or on TV wildlife programs.

[01:43] AUDIO: The central idea behind the Chimp Paradox is that the human brain consists of two components, which the author calls the human part and the chimp part. Let me explain what he means. So the human, this is the aspect of ourselves that on the whole tends to be sensible. It analyzes things that happen before actually deciding what to do.

[02:08] AUDIO: It's situated in the frontal lobe of the brain. And one thing about the human part is that it just loves it when there are rules in place because these can simply be followed and it knows what to do. And the other side of ourselves, of course, is the chimp part. Now, compared to the human, the way that the chimp responds is very emotional.

[02:33] AUDIO: And Peter's central message is that, basically, the chimp can either be our best friend or our worst enemy. That's what he means when he talks about the Chimp Paradox, because having these completely distinct personalities can frequently be the cause of a conflict. So I'd like to provide a couple of examples of what the Chimp Paradox might look like in practice. So in the book, Peters provides the example of a person going into a room, maybe at a party, and finding that all the other people there are strangers.

[03:09] AUDIO: So the chimp within us may feel insecure or even panic, while our inner human reacts differently and decides how best to deal with the situation. Another example of the Chimp Paradox would be if you have a repetitive chore that needs doing, say, decorating a room in your apartment. But suppose that then a friend contacts you and gives you the chance to socialize instead. Now, that's an offer that might be very tempting for your inner chimp.

[03:41] AUDIO: So you've got this dilemma, this choice, that needs to be made. And you're being pulled in two different directions, by the human part of your brain in one direction and by your chimp part in the other. I'd like to turn now to the world of sport, because that's where the lessons of the Chimp Paradox have been widely applied, often very successfully. If you look online to read about Steve Peters and the Chimp Paradox, you'll see quite a bit of discussion about a very prominent cyclist who was close to quitting.

[04:14] AUDIO: But then reading the book gave her the determination to carry on, which she did. In fact, she has publicly endorsed the mindset that the book prescribes. And she credits it with having enabled her to become not just a top athlete, she was that anyway, but a champion. And her career really has gone from strength to strength.

[04:36] AUDIO: And that's by no means the only example of the lessons of the Chimp Paradox being applied in elite sports. Top snooker player Ronnie O'Sullivan, who turned professional at the age of 16, has been troubled by depression throughout his career. But Steve Peters was able to guide O'Sullivan and help him find ways to cope using the human chimp psychology presented in the book. And to continue playing at the very highest level at an age when many other snooker players had retired.

[05:09] AUDIO: One of the methods he used was to make sure that O'Sullivan made space in his schedule to go running, as this was an activity he'd been keen on for years. But it was something that he often found he was too busy to do. So, anyway, that's a brief introduction to the ideas behind the Chimp Paradox and how they've been applied in sport. Are there any questions?

transcript: [00:50] Officer: Good afternoon madam, how can I help you?
[00:52] Chloe: Oh, hello. I think my passport has been stolen and the embassy told me to register it with you.

[00:59] Officer: Sorry to hear that, madam. Let me find a form to take some details. OK, here we are. So, I need to take some information about you and what happened, and then I can give you a crime reference number to give to your embassy.
[01:15] Officer: OK, right, let's start with the information on the passport. What's your surname?
[01:22] Chloe: It's Miss Walsh, that's W-A-L-S-H.
[01:27] Officer: And your first name?
[01:29] Chloe: Chloe.
[01:31] Officer: OK, Miss Walsh. And can I take your date of birth?
[01:35] Chloe: Yes, it's the 5th of July, 1987.
[01:39] Officer: OK, I've got that here. And next I'm going to need to take your place of birth.
[01:45] Chloe: I was born in Ireland.
[01:47] Officer: I need the city or town, madam.
[01:49] Chloe: Oh, it was the capital, Dublin.
[01:52] Officer: And do you know your passport number?
[01:55] Chloe: Um, I have a copy of it somewhere. Oh, yes, here you go. It's 323682.
[02:06] Officer: Now I need to take some contact details in case we need to contact you or if we find the passport. Can I take your phone number?
[02:14] Chloe: Yes, my mobile number is 07780 367021.
[02:22] Officer: So that's 07780 367012.
[02:30] Chloe: No, it ends 021.
[02:33] Officer: OK, and your email address?
[02:36] Chloe: It's chloe.walsh at email.com.
[02:41] Officer: And finally, can I take your address, please?
[02:45] Chloe: It's 97 East Street in Brighton and the postcode is BN12SE.
[03:34] Officer: OK, now I need to make a few notes about what happened. You say that your passport was stolen?
[03:41] Chloe: Well, I'm not sure. It was either stolen from my pocket or I dropped it and lost it.
[03:47] Officer: OK, madam. Well, you need to report it with us whether it was lost or stolen. You said that it was in your pocket?
[03:55] Chloe: That's right. I kept it in the pocket of my jacket because I thought it would be safer there.
[03:59] Officer: OK, well there has been a number of people reporting pickpocketing recently, so maybe it was stolen from your pocket. When was this?
[04:09] Chloe: It was last Wednesday.
[04:11] Officer: So that's Wednesday the 21st of July?
[04:14] Chloe: That's right.
[04:15] Officer: And do you know where it happened?
[04:17] Chloe: Well, I'm not sure exactly. In the afternoon I went to meet a friend and I know I had it with me then because I felt it in my pocket before I left.
[04:27] Officer: And where did you meet your friend?
[04:29] Chloe: In a green cafe on the high street.
[04:32] Officer: And what did you do after that?

[04:34] Chloe: So, I went for a walk along the high street and was going to walk home but it started raining so I decided to get the bus home. I think I got home around 4.30 and it was then that I realised I didn't have my passport with me anymore.
[04:50] Officer: That's all the information that I need. I'll give you a crime reference number now which they might ask you for when you get your new passport. The number is A13-5970.
[05:05] Chloe: OK. Well, thanks for your help.
[05:08] Officer: No problem, madam. Have a nice day.

passages.title: River Avon Adventures
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "River Avon Adventures"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:47] AUDIO: Hello everyone. Welcome to River Avon Adventures. My name's Amanda and in a few moments you'll be getting into our kayaks and going out on the River Avon. Now what's great about the boats you'll be in today is that once you're in and seated, you'll very quickly notice that there's plenty of space to move your legs around in, so you can position yourself in whatever way feels right for you.

[01:14] AUDIO: The boats are very safe and people don't usually fall in, but in theory it might happen. So you need to know what to do. Now it is difficult to get back on the boat in deep water, so don't try that. Just stay by your boat and someone will come and sort you out.

[01:33] AUDIO: Avoid trying to swim to the land or you may get in the way of someone else's boat. As for what to do with your phones while you're on the water and whether they're best left in the car for safety, well, the car park isn't monitored and if you did leave your phone behind, you'd end up with no photos of your day on the river. So we actually have little plastic boxes for you, like those ones for storing food. It's worth using one and putting your device in just to be on the safe side.

[02:04] AUDIO: Phones don't float of course, but these do. Now we'd love to welcome you back to River Avon Adventures again in the future. We're open all year, even in winter. And it's not just kayaks that we rent out.

[02:20] AUDIO: We also have wetsuits, stand-up paddle boards and fishing gear. And binoculars if you want to try a bit of bird watching. Lots of great stuff for you to have a go with. And the good news is we can offer discounts for next time you come to River Avon Adventures.

[02:36] AUDIO: All you have to do is tell your friends that you've enjoyed your trip with us and when they join our mailing list and mention you, you'll get a voucher for 20% off. Okay, we're nearly ready. You'll be going off in your boats soon. I'm just going to show you on this map what routes you can take today.

[03:36] AUDIO: So we're at the boathouse here on the south side of the river in the middle of the map. And the campsite, as you can see, is directly across the river from here on the opposite bank. The river's current is very gentle, so you can paddle either way. If you start going east, that's toward the right on the map.

[03:55] AUDIO: You'll soon come to the fish restaurant. It's on your left after you go under the old stone bridge. There's space to moor your boat if you want to stop for lunch. Or you might prefer to have a picnic of your own.

[04:08] AUDIO: And there's also a really good spot for that with benches for you to sit on. And you'll find this where the river splits in two. So when you're having your sandwiches, you'll actually be on your very own island. If you need a toilet, you'll have to go to the west of where we are now.

[04:25] AUDIO: If you see how the car park is almost surrounded by the river, well, the loos are on the far side of the car park from here. So just beyond it, in other words, but on the same side of the water. The south side, I mean. It's just by the sharp bend in the river.

[04:43] AUDIO: And then we have Frog Rock. That's a rock in the shape of a frog. At least some people think it is. So to get there, when you're travelling west and you see a wooden bridge, there are some rocks there.
[04:57] AUDIO: But that's not Frog Rock. You need to keep going, and then it's on the right after you go under the bridge.

passages.title: Cotman’s paintings
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Cotman’s paintings"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:53] Paul: All right, Sue, do you want to work with me on this presentation we need to give next week?
[00:59] Sue: Hey, Paul, sure. So we've got to talk about one artist and show up to six of their artworks.
[01:06] Paul: Yes, that's right. We could talk about John Sell Cotman.
[01:11] Sue: The English watercolor painter from the 1800s.
[01:14] Paul: That's the one. You can tell a Cotman painting as soon as you see one.
[01:19] Sue: Definitely. I mean, he painted landscapes and architecture just like his contemporaries, but Cotman had this unique way of applying color.

[01:28] Paul: Yes, he'd put on one layer of paint, let it dry, then do another layer on top of that to make the color more intense. So regardless of whether he signed the picture, you immediately know it's a Cotman.
[01:41] Sue: Yep. Thing is, when we present to the other students, well, Cotman, he's not exactly Van Gogh, is he? As in, he's not a world-famous painter who had a huge influence.
[01:55] Paul: Exactly. You and I were both familiar with him, but not everybody will be. So we can't assume any prior knowledge.
[02:03] Sue: Sure. I read that he often stayed somewhere called Bransby, but I'm not aware he ever painted Bransby, so I'm not sure why he went.

[02:12] Paul: Oh, he stayed with friends who owned a house there when he was on painting tours, and they introduced him to wealthy people who would offer him work, maybe to paint their portrait or whatever.
[02:23] Sue: I see. So he was on the lookout for his next commission.
[02:27] Paul: Right. It was in his interest to keep getting invited back. Shall we focus on Cotman's friendships in our talk, his love life and family?
[02:37] Sue: Personalize it. Make our classmates feel they're getting to know Cotman, the man. What do you think?

[02:44] Paul: Well, we could in theory go through some of the letters he wrote. I mean, plenty of them have survived, but to be honest, that might be off-topic. And it would take ages. I say we keep to the brief and limit ourselves to his artworks.
[02:58] Paul: Make sure our audience knows what makes his paintings so fascinating.
[03:03] Sue: Okay.
[03:47] Paul: Okay, so our presentation can show six Cotman paintings.
[03:51] Sue: Yeah, and we can research more and decide what to say about each one we choose.

[03:56] Paul: One good example is his painting of that tall stone bridge, Chirk Aqueduct. At least that's what it's called. Thing is though, the actual aqueduct at Chirk doesn't look anything like it.
[04:09] Sue: The proportions are totally different.
[04:12] Paul: Right. So maybe it's actually somewhere else entirely.
[04:16] Sue: Maybe Cotman got it wrong when he was naming the picture.
[04:19] Paul: Hmm. Let's check that.
[04:22] Sue: Okay. And then there's Inrokerby Park.
[04:25] Paul: It's atmospheric, but doesn't have much detail.
[04:29] Sue: Was it left unfinished, do you think?
[04:31] Paul: If we compare it to some of his other landscapes, we might be able to tell.
[04:36] Sue: Yes, let's do that.
[04:38] Paul: And then there's his painting of Bedlam Furnace. It shows the way that many English towns in the early 1800s were industrializing, completely transforming the urban landscape.
[04:48] Sue: Yeah, factory chimneys spewing out dark smoke. Total contrast to all those rural scenes he painted.
[04:56] Paul: Yeah. Is that his only portrayal of heavy industry?
[05:00] Sue: Possibly. I'm not aware of any more.
[05:03] Paul: We can do a quick search, see if there are.
[05:06] Sue: Okay. Oh, another one to show is Croyland Abbey.
[05:10] Paul: Oh, that's the one where, when he was on site, making a sketch of the building. I think there was some incident.
[05:17] Sue: Didn't he get involved in a fight with a passerby?
[05:20] Paul: You're joking.
[05:21] Sue: I only have a vague memory of reading about it. I'll have to look it up.
[05:25] Paul: Yeah, and let me know. And we could show the kitchen.
[05:29] Sue: It's an interior view, quite unusual for Cotman. That features a couple of seated figures by the kitchen table.
[05:36] Paul: I wonder if they're Cotman's family.
[05:39] Sue: Could be.
[05:40] Paul: I've got a book on Cotman. I'll see if that says anything about their possible identity.
[05:46] Sue: Good idea.
[05:47] Paul: Another interesting picture is Doorway at Riveau. Supposedly painted in 1803, when Cotman was just 21.
[05:56] Sue: But the thing is, it looks more like his mature style. So I wonder if it was actually done later.
[06:03] Paul: When he was older.
[06:05] Sue: Yeah, and his style had evolved.
[06:08] Paul: Not sure if we'll find any evidence about that, but we can try.
[06:12] Sue: Great.

passages.title: Greek fire
content: 📌 Greek fire
Greek fire = a chemical weapon developed in the 7th century by the Byzantines (who lived around modern-day Istanbul)
Fighting with Greek fire
Byzantine armies used Greek fire to burn their enemies' [ _____ ]
Greek fire was able to burn on [ _____ ]
One of the few things that could stop Greek fire from burning was [ _____ ]
To make Greek fire, the inflammable liquid was put into [ _____ ], which were fired at the enemy.
Making Greek fire
The process of making Greek fire was a [ _____ ]
Likely ingredients of Greek fire:
resin from [ _____ ]trees (which made Greek fire sticky)sulphur[ _____ ]
A ninth-century Bulgarian army tried to [ _____ ] Greek fire, but were unsuccessful.
How Greek fire was described in contemporary reports
Byzantine Emperor Leo the Sixth said that using Greek fire caused a lot of [ _____ ]
Lord of Joinville described the sudden [ _____ ] that accompanied Greek fire.
transcript: [01:12] AUDIO: Hello everyone. Today I'd like to continue our lecture series on medieval warfare. I shall be telling you today about a weapon known as Greek fire, which was an early form of chemical weapon dating back to around the 7th century. It was most probably developed by the Byzantines, the people who lived around what is now Istanbul in Turkey.

[01:39] AUDIO: Now in battle, Greek fire enabled the Byzantines to set fire to the ships of whoever they were fighting against and to do so from a distance. This gave them a massive military advantage over their enemies. We do know that Greek fire was a terrifying weapon that proved particularly effective because unlike the majority of substances, when it came into contact with water, it would just carry on burning. It also had the property of sticking to whatever it touched.

[02:15] AUDIO: So you see, what made Greek fire such a devastating weapon is that once it was burning, it was incredibly difficult to extinguish. Vinegar seems to have worked, but this isn't likely to have been something that was readily available to the average medieval soldier in the middle of a battle. And so anyone under attack from Greek fire really had very limited options in terms of actually putting the flames out. The inflammable substance that we refer to as Greek fire was actually liquid in form and it was packed into pots, which were then shot into the air and towards the enemy using a catapult.

[03:02] AUDIO: These would then shatter when they landed and the area affected would burst into flames, often with devastating effect. So, what did Greek fire consist of and how was it made? Well, the answer is that we don't really know for sure. The reason that so little is known is that the actual composition of Greek fire had to be a secret because the Byzantines, understandably, didn't want to lose the military advantage that it gave them.

[03:34] AUDIO: So, we have to try and work out as best we can what the raw materials might have been and how the Byzantines produced it. One thing we know is that the substance was sticky and it is likely that resin was obtained from wood in the pine forests which covered so much of the Byzantines' territory at the time. This was almost certainly used to make Greek fire. Clearly, access to the raw materials needed to produce it was absolutely essential and one of these was sulphur.

[04:09] AUDIO: The Byzantines also controlled areas where oil can be found close to the surface of the earth so this was almost certainly another of the key components. One key objective for the Byzantines in any military campaign was to prevent the Greek fire from being captured by the enemy. However, in the year 812, an army from Bulgaria managed to do just that. They removed some Greek fire intact and unburned.

[04:43] AUDIO: But, however hard they tried, they were unable to copy it. If they had managed, well, we can only guess whether that could have affected the balance of power in the region. There are some surviving contemporary reports of Greek fire and I'd like to start around the year 900 with an account by the Byzantine emperor Leo VI perhaps writing to intimidate potential enemies who described the enormous amount of smoke that would appear whenever Greek fire was discharged by his army. Another account is from Lord of Joinville, a writer from France who lived in the 13th century.

[05:26] AUDIO: He described the absolutely deafening noise there would be all of a sudden whenever Greek fire was used. When you read these contemporary accounts, presumably from people describing what they themselves had witnessed, it really gets across how terrifying Greek fire must have been.

questions.prompt: Byzantine armies used Greek fire to burn their enemies' _____

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "Now in battle, Greek fire enabled the Byzantines to set fire to the ships of whoever they were fighting against and to do so from a distance."
explanation.step3: ▶️ Thông tin cần nghe ở : “Greek fire enabled the Byzantines to set fire to…” ☺️ Cùng xem giải thích nhé : Trong bài nghe, người nói đề cập rõ rằng quân đội Byzantine dùng Greek fire để đốt cháy các ships (tàu) của kẻ địch từ xa ("set fire to the ships of whoever they were fighting against"). Từ cần điền chắc chắn là danh từ số nhiều ships . ✅ Đáp án đúng: ships 🧐 Lưu ý bẫy đề thi : ❌ soldiers => Từ này có thể gây nhầm lẫn vì bài nghe nói tới “medieval soldier” (lính thời trung cổ), tuy nhiên từ soldiers không phải đối tượng bị đốt cháy được nhắc trực tiếp. ❌ forests => Đây là một từ xuất hiện trong bài nói ("pine forests"), tuy nhiên nó được đề cập ở phần nói về nguyên liệu chế tạo Greek fire, không liên quan tới đối tượng bị đốt.

explanation.step3: ▶️ Thông tin cần nghe ở : "unlike the majority of substances, when it came into contact with..." ☺️ Cùng xem giải thích nhé : Bài nghe nêu rõ rằng, điểm đặc biệt của Greek fire là nó vẫn có thể tiếp tục cháy khi tiếp xúc với water (nước) , điều khác biệt so với đa số các chất khác ("when it came into contact with water, it would just carry on burning"). ✅ Đáp án đúng: water 🧐 Lưu ý bẫy đề thi : ❌ air => Đây là từ thông thường có thể nghĩ tới nhưng không đúng, vì trong bài nói không hề đề cập việc Greek fire cháy nhờ không khí. ❌ land => Đề cập tới đất hay nơi tiếp đất nhưng bài nói không hề nhấn mạnh điểm này như là một khả năng đặc biệt của Greek fire.

Như vậy, đáp án chắc chắn là vinegar . ✅ Đáp án đúng: vinegar 🧐 Lưu ý bẫy đề thi : ❌ water => Dễ gây nhầm lẫn, vì bài nghe trước đó nhắc tới nước (water), nhưng thực chất nước làm Greek fire cháy mạnh hơn chứ không dập được lửa. ❌ oil => Dầu cũng được nhắc tới trong bài, nhưng là nguyên liệu chế tạo, không phải chất dập tắt lửa.

questions.prompt: To make Greek fire, the inflammable liquid was put into _____, which were fired at the enemy.

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "The inflammable substance that we refer to as Greek fire was actually liquid in form and it was packed into pots, which were then shot into the air and towards the enemy using a catapult."

questions.prompt: The process of making Greek fire was a _____

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "The reason that so little is known is that the actual composition of Greek fire had to be a secret because the Byzantines, understandably, didn't want to lose the military advantage that it gave them."
explanation.step3: ▶️ Thông tin cần nghe ở : "the actual composition of Greek fire had to be a…" ☺️ Cùng xem giải thích nhé : Bài nghe nêu rất rõ, việc sản xuất Greek fire là một secret (bí mật) , bởi người Byzantine muốn bảo vệ lợi thế quân sự của họ ("the actual composition of Greek fire had to be a secret..."). Do đó, đáp án đúng là secret . ✅ Đáp án đúng: secret 🧐 Lưu ý bẫy đề thi : ❌ advantage => Có thể gây nhầm lẫn vì bài nghe cũng nhắc tới "military advantage", tuy nhiên đây là lý do chứ không phải bản chất của quá trình chế tạo Greek fire. ❌ weapon => Greek fire đúng là vũ khí nhưng đây không phải là từ chỉ bản chất của việc sản xuất.

questions.prompt: resin from _____trees (which made Greek fire sticky)sulphur_____

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "One thing we know is that the substance was sticky and it is likely that resin was obtained from wood in the pine forests which covered so much of the Byzantines' territory at the time."
explanation.step3: ▶️ Thông tin cần nghe ở : "resin was obtained from wood in the…" ☺️ Cùng xem giải thích nhé : Trong bài nghe có nhắc tới việc người Byzantine thu nhựa ( resin ) từ cây gỗ trong các khu rừng pine (thông) : "resin was obtained from wood in the pine forests ...". Đề bài đã cho sẵn từ trees , vậy đáp án đúng cần điền vào chỉ là tên loại cây này: pine . ✅ Đáp án đúng: pine 🧐 Lưu ý bẫy đề thi : ❌ wood => "wood" được nhắc trong bài nghe, nhưng đây không phải loại cây cụ thể mà chỉ là "gỗ" chung chung. ❌ forests => Đây là nơi cây thông mọc, nhưng đề bài hỏi tên loại cây cụ thể, nên không thể chọn "forests".

questions.prompt: A ninth-century Bulgarian army tried to _____ Greek fire, but were unsuccessful.

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "The Byzantines also controlled areas where oil can be found close to the surface of the earth so this was almost certainly another of the key components."
explanation.step3: ▶️ Thông tin cần nghe ở : "The Byzantines also controlled areas where…" ☺️ Cùng xem giải thích nhé : Trong bài nghe đề cập rõ ràng rằng ngoài resin và sulphur, một thành phần quan trọng nữa là oil (dầu) ("The Byzantines also controlled areas where oil can be found... another of the key components"). Vậy đáp án đúng là oil . ✅ Đáp án đúng: oil 🧐 Lưu ý bẫy đề thi : ❌ water => Được nhắc tới nhưng là chất khiến Greek fire cháy mạnh hơn, không phải nguyên liệu. ❌ wood => Chỉ được nhắc như nguồn cung cấp resin, không phải nguyên liệu trực tiếp để làm Greek fire.

questions.prompt: Byzantine Emperor Leo the Sixth said that using Greek fire caused a lot of _____

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "However, in the year 812, an army from Bulgaria managed to do just that. They removed some Greek fire intact and unburned. But, however hard they tried, they were unable to copy it."
explanation.step3: ▶️ Thông tin cần nghe ở : "in the year 812, an army from Bulgaria managed to..." ☺️ Cùng xem giải thích nhé : Trong bài nghe có nói rõ quân đội Bulgaria vào năm 812 đã cố gắng copy (sao chép) Greek fire nhưng không thành công ("they were unable to copy it"). Như vậy, đáp án đúng chắc chắn là copy . ✅ Đáp án đúng: copy 🧐 Lưu ý bẫy đề thi : ❌ capture => Từ này có thể gây nhầm lẫn vì quân đội Bulgaria cũng được nhắc tới việc "captured" (chiếm được) Greek fire. Nhưng đề bài hỏi hành động mà họ cố làm nhưng thất bại ("unsuccessful"), nên "copy" chính xác hơn. ❌ use => Từ này cũng dễ gây nhầm lẫn nhưng bài nghe không đề cập việc họ cố gắng "use" (sử dụng), mà chỉ nói rõ họ cố gắng "copy" lại vũ khí này.

questions.prompt: Lord of Joinville described the sudden _____ that accompanied Greek fire.

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "There are some surviving contemporary reports of Greek fire and I'd like to start around the year 900 with an account by the Byzantine emperor Leo VI perhaps writing to intimidate potential enemies who described the enormous amount of smoke that would appear whenever Greek fire was discharged by his army."
explanation.step3: ▶️ Thông tin cần nghe ở : “the enormous amount of…” ☺️ Cùng xem giải thích nhé : Trong bài nghe có nhắc đến lời của hoàng đế Byzantine Leo VI, ông mô tả rằng khi Greek fire được sử dụng thì có một lượng rất lớn smoke (khói) xuất hiện ("the enormous amount of smoke that would appear whenever Greek fire was discharged"). Đáp án đúng là smoke . ✅ Đáp án đúng: smoke 🧐 Lưu ý bẫy đề thi : ❌ fire => Có thể gây nhầm lẫn, nhưng đề bài và bài nghe đang nói tới một thứ khác ngoài lửa, cụ thể là "smoke". ❌ noise => Được nhắc tới trong phần sau của bài nghe (do người khác mô tả), không phải trong đoạn của Leo VI.

questions.prompt: resin from _____trees (which made Greek fire sticky)sulphur_____

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "Another account is from Lord of Joinville, a writer from France who lived in the 13th century. He described the absolutely deafening noise there would be all of a sudden whenever Greek fire was used."
explanation.step3: ▶️ Thông tin cần nghe ở : “Lord of Joinville described the absolutely…” ☺️ Cùng xem giải thích nhé : Trong bài nghe, Lord of Joinville đã mô tả rõ rằng khi Greek fire được sử dụng thì có một noise (tiếng động) cực kỳ lớn và đột ngột ("the absolutely deafening noise there would be all of a sudden whenever Greek fire was used"). Đáp án đúng chắc chắn là noise . ✅ Đáp án đúng: noise 🧐 Lưu ý bẫy đề thi : ❌ smoke => Được mô tả bởi Leo VI, không phải bởi Joinville. ❌ fire => Tuy Greek fire liên quan tới lửa, nhưng bài nghe của Joinville nhấn mạnh đặc biệt tới âm thanh ("noise") chứ không phải lửa.

transcript: [00:50] Receptionist: Good morning, Holiday Plus Hotel, Easthaven. Can I help you?
[00:54] Susan: Oh yes, hello. I just spoke to a couple of rooms online and I think I made a mistake. Can I change it with you?
[01:02] Receptionist: Of course you can. Could you give me your surname please?
[01:05] Susan: It's Connor. C-O-N-N-O-R.
[01:09] Receptionist: Thank you. And your first name?
[01:12] Susan: It's Susan.
[01:13] Receptionist: I'll have a look for you. Can you confirm your arrival date?
[01:17] Susan: It's the 28th of June.
[01:20] Receptionist: Okay, I've found you here. So that's a family of two adults and one child leaving on the 6th of July, which is a total of seven nights. Is that correct?
[01:30] Susan: Oh no, I don't think so. It's eight, isn't it? Arriving on the Thursday and leaving the following Friday?
[01:37] Receptionist: You're quite right. Sorry, my mistake. So you said that you wanted to make changes to your booking. Is it the rooms that you wanted to change?
[01:45] Susan: If possible, yes please.
[01:46] Receptionist: Your reservation is currently for one double room and one single.
[01:50] Susan: Yes, I still need the double room, but I'd like a twin room instead of the single. You see, my daughter's friend's going to be joining us.
[01:57] Receptionist: Okay, let me just check availability. Yes, we can do that for you.
[02:04] Susan: Great.
[02:05] Receptionist: Or alternatively, could I make a suggestion?
[02:08] Susan: Sure.
[02:09] Receptionist: Have you considered a family suite? I think you'd be much more comfortable than in the two rooms.
[02:14] Susan: So what do you get with the suite?

[02:16] Receptionist: You'd have the two bedrooms that you've requested as well as a living room. This would also guarantee that your rooms are together and not spread out over the hotel, and you'd get a terrace to enjoy the sun.
[02:28] Susan: I see. I'm not sure about that to be honest. It sounds expensive.

[03:11] Receptionist: Actually, the suites tend to work out as better value than having two individual rooms. I'll just check to see what the charge would be to upgrade. Okay, you've paid £863 for your original booking, so it would be another £39 because the suite would be £902.
[03:31] Susan: Oh, so I'd need to pay the difference?
[03:34] Receptionist: Exactly, but you can do that on arrival at the hotel.
[03:37] Susan: Great.
[03:38] Receptionist: Okay, now do any of the party have any special requirements?
[03:42] Susan: Yes, my husband is a wheelchair user, so obviously we'll have to have that with us.
[03:47] Receptionist: Of course, I'll make note of that, but the hotel is fully accessible, and staff are always available if there's anything that can be done to make your stay more comfortable.
[03:56] Susan: I appreciate that. Oh, and one other thing, my daughter's friend has a fish allergy.
[04:01] Receptionist: Fine, I'll make note of that, but they'll need to mention it to restaurant staff when they're here.
[04:07] Susan: Oh, one more thing. I entered my phone number when I made the original booking, but can I give you my husband's as well, just in case?
[04:15] Receptionist: Yes, please.
[04:23] Receptionist: Got that. Thank you very much, and we look forward to seeing you here.
[04:27] Susan: Thank you.

passages.title: Museum about how ordinary people lived in the past
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Museum about how ordinary people lived in the past"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:49] AUDIO: Hello everyone, welcome to the Arvington Museum of Work. Let's start with some background. Now this wonderful old building that we're in was unoccupied for many years, but the council were very keen to protect it and so decided to give it a new purpose by converting it into something that would benefit the many people who were already visiting the town each year. The council paid for the whole renovation themselves and we've been lucky that other museums from all around the country have lent us objects from their collections which are on display here.

[01:25] AUDIO: The main purpose of the museum really has always been to demonstrate to people that learning about the past can be enjoyable and even exciting and I hope that comes across. I also hope this will be your first of many visits to our museum. As you know it's free to get in which we're really proud of. Now on your next visit you'll probably still see the same exhibitions but I always think that even when you look at something you've seen before you can always find out more about it than you did the first time.

[01:57] AUDIO: And our exhibitions are good, believe me. We've won awards for the region's best interactive displays. Oh by the way, I should just mention that the cafe is closed for renovation at the moment but should hopefully be open by the next time you come and I strongly recommend trying out their cakes. Let me tell you about some of the areas you'll walk through.

[03:08] AUDIO: The museum is set up so that you walk through displays that take you back through different periods in Arvington's history and see how people lived. Starting with the forge you can go back 1,000 years in time and see how skilled workers crafted everyday objects out of wood and metal. But we don't just tell you about it, we get you to do it yourself so you'll get experience of carefully crafting a useful object like a knife. And then in the market one of our historical interpreters will be there in person telling you what it was like to work on a farm growing produce like wheat and vegetables and then carry it all over very long distances to a market to try and sell.

[03:53] AUDIO: You can ask the interpreters questions of course and you'll find they're very knowledgeable. Staying with the subject of food, the next area in the museum is the bakery where we make the kinds of foods that local people would have eaten in the past using the original cooking techniques. These are on sale there for you to try. The recipes and cooking methods may be ancient but 21st century forms of payment are accepted.

[04:20] AUDIO: Next on the tour is the building zone where you have the chance for a sit down to enjoy the spectacular time lapse animated movie of Arvington developing over the last 1,000 years from a tiny village into the town we have today. It's just three minutes long but you can view it as many times as you like. After that you'll come to the hall, a space that's devoted to the clothing industry which was a huge part of the economy of Arvington and the surrounding area in the past. You can find out how clothing was made when everything was done by hand and you can have a go at helping one of our historical interpreters to make a piece of clothing yourself.

[05:03] AUDIO: So if you never knew how to sew a button back onto a shirt you might find it useful. Finally the tour ends down in the basement where there's a wide variety of merchandise available including books and toys. A final tip, download the museum app and you get an introductory discount voucher which you can use on purchases in the basement as well as commentaries on all the exhibits in the museum. Anyway, enjoy your visit.

passages.title: Humboldt's books
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Humboldt's books"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [01:00] Martin: Hi Anna, shall we talk about our research for our history of environmentalism unit?
[01:06] Anna: Oh hi Martin, sure.
[01:08] Martin: So we agreed we'd give a presentation about Alexander von Humboldt, didn't we?
[01:13] Anna: Yes, did you know much about him?
[01:16] Martin: I knew that he was a German explorer and scientist and that he lived in the 1800s, and you?
[01:22] Anna: Well, that, and that he travelled extensively around South America, written lots of books, and been hugely famous.
[01:31] Martin: During his lifetime, yes, but these days he's largely forgotten.
[01:34] Anna: You think so?

[01:35] Martin: Yeah, which is a shame really. I mean, it's not like he had these theories which turned out to be wrong, far from it. He was saying things which at the time were groundbreaking, but now it's just stuff that we accept as being self-evident.
[01:50] Anna: And having stated the obvious, I suppose you could say that's hardly grounds for remaining famous.
[01:56] Martin: I mean, he argued that it's essential to respect the natural world rather than just exploit it by mining and polluting, which we take for granted now.
[02:05] Anna: Sure, I've heard him described as the father of environmentalism.

[02:09] Martin: Right. And I suppose that's because of his view that in the natural world everything is connected. So in one location there might be a particular animal which has evolved to feed on a particular plant. As a result, the plant will develop its own defence mechanism.

[02:25] Martin: If one species changes in some way, then others are likely to in response. Changes in the environment tend to have knock-on effects, and Humboldt brought that to people's attention, really very convincingly.

[02:37] Anna: Yeah, I've heard that during his lifetime he was one of the most famous people on the planet. Which seems odd, because he was just a largely self-taught academic, writing in great detail about all these obscure scientific topics, which can't have had much to do with the lives of ordinary people.
[02:55] Martin: Ah, but it was the diversity of subjects, from volcanoes to ocean currents, where Humboldt probably knew more than anyone alive.
[03:03] Anna: Possibly, yeah.
[03:04] Martin: That's what made him such a big name. Even kings and presidents wanted to meet him. And his books sold really well.

[03:11] Anna: I think some of them were quite dense and hard to follow, but they combined both scientific research and some very flowery language, poetic even. Very different from conventional academic writing these days, of course, where writers just stick to the facts. But back then, it was what people liked.
[03:29] Martin: Right. I suppose Humboldt's books were like an early version of Wikipedia.
[03:33] Anna: Ha! You mean because of all these collaborators, who'd produce a bit of text for his latest book and send it to him.
[03:39] Martin: Exactly.
[03:40] Anna: So he'd assemble all these bits that he got from other people.
[03:44] Martin: Right. One amazing thing about Humboldt is that he wasn't just a scientist, he was also a social critic.
[03:51] Anna: Well, in theory, yes. But I read that when he met Thomas Jefferson...
[03:55] Martin: President of the United States.

[03:58] Anna: Yeah, who actually kept slaves. And Humboldt had argued very strongly against slavery, describing it as inhumane. But when he and Jefferson met, Humboldt deliberately avoided the issue of slavery so that they wouldn't argue, which was a waste of an opportunity to take Jefferson to task over his decision to use slaves. A bit cowardly, maybe, if he was so principled.
[04:23] Martin: Fair point. So, in our talk, why don't we link the places Humboldt travelled to what he accomplished while he was there?

[05:05] Anna: Good idea. I read that when Humboldt visited Lake Valencia, he was told by local residents that the area had got a whole lot drier in recent years. So he investigated and concluded that it was because of what people were doing to the landscape.
[05:21] Martin: Right, hadn't there been cutting down loads of trees?
[05:24] Anna: Exactly, which dried out the land so there was less rain. So people's interactions with their environment were actually altering the weather.

[05:33] Martin: Which we know about now, but he worked it out 200 years ago. Right, and when he climbed Mount Chimborazo, aiming to identify what plants grew at different altitudes, he developed acute mountain sickness. But having such a keen, analytical mind, he was able to conclude that it must have been due to low oxygen levels at higher altitudes.
[05:55] Anna: Interesting.
[05:56] Martin: Again, common knowledge now.
[05:58] Anna: But not back then.
[06:00] Martin: True.
[06:01] Anna: I read that during his time in Cuba, as well as studying the wildlife, he also analysed the technology in trade.
[06:08] Martin: Sugar production, you mean.
[06:09] Anna: That's right. Then he made suggestions as to how it could be enhanced, so as to be more profitable.

[06:15] Martin: Wow. And in Venezuela, hadn't he heard rumours of a natural waterway that supposedly connected two separate river systems? It's just that such things are rare, and he wanted to verify if it really existed.
[06:28] Anna: That's right. The Casiquiere Canal, I think it's called.
[06:32] Martin: Yeah, well, sure enough, he found it and mapped it.
[06:35] Anna: What an amazing guy.

transcript: [01:10] AUDIO: In today's introduction to seismology lecture we'll be looking at predicting volcanic eruptions. The destruction caused by a large volcano can be devastating and with more of them being increasingly surrounded by urban areas it is more important than ever before to be able to predict and plan for an eruption. After all there's no way to prevent this massive natural force. So what can we do to predict when a volcano is going to erupt?

[01:41] AUDIO: The first sign that we need to look for is earthquakes. In the run-up to an eruption there are often hundreds of small earthquakes caused by magma rising up through cracks in the earth's crust. As magma comes into contact with rocks they crack which causes a mini earthquake. And now many of these earthquakes are too small to be detected by people which is why the ground around earthquakes in densely populated areas needs to be constantly monitored by seismometers.

[02:14] AUDIO: These are instruments which measure the motion of the earth's surface and a higher frequency of these earthquakes could indicate an upcoming eruption. Another important area which needs to be monitored is the temperature around volcanoes. There are lots of volcanic features like steam vents, geysers and hot springs that are expected to be consistently hot but any spikes in this could indicate dangerous volcanic activity. Technology has had a huge impact on the way we collate this data.

[02:47] AUDIO: The safest way for us to assess this is to take images using satellites as collecting this data from the ground can be hazardous. In addition to the frequency and size of earthquakes the final indicator that we assess is the atmospheric conditions around the volcano. Now most active volcanoes release a range of gases but higher than normal rates of sulfur and carbon dioxide emissions can reveal a lot about the magma system of the volcano and could also be a telltale sign of danger. In order for this to be monitored gas samples need to be taken and checked using a spectrometer which are types of chemical sensors.

[03:29] AUDIO: These monitoring techniques are becoming increasingly advanced and some earthquakes like Mount St Helens in the US and Mount Vesuvius in Italy are monitored 24 hours a day by teams of scientists for the safety of the inhabitants living around them. However understanding and predicting when a blast is imminent is only the first stage in keeping people safe. We also need to have an effective emergency plan prepared. When faced with a major volcanic incident authorities need to take a number of steps to reduce civilian casualties.

[04:05] AUDIO: The first is to calculate an exclusion zone around a volcano where an eruption is imminent. This would stop anyone from entering the area. The size of the zone would vary depending on the predicted scale of eruption. There is one in effect in Montserrat which has been in place since 1995.

[04:26] AUDIO: In addition to stopping people entering the zone authorities need to be ready to get people out. Being prepared for a large-scale evacuation is key as people will be panicking and major transit routes will be quickly blocked. All of this costs money so obviously a government needs to have the funds to deal with emergencies. Having an advanced communication system in place is a must in order to notify people of both the dangers and the action that is being taken.

[04:59] AUDIO: Finally it is important to know that an eruption could occur at any time. Citizens living near particularly active volcanoes need to be educated about both emergency procedures and also the basic provisions that they will need to keep in their house to assist them in times of emergency. Now let's look in more detail at the design of a seismometer.

transcript: [00:51] Staff: Hello, Henbridge College. Can I help you?
[00:54] Woman: Hello. I saw a course on your website that I'm interested in. It was about creating jewelry. The thing is, though, I wasn't able to reserve a place.
[01:04] Woman: Are you able to help me with that?
[01:06] Staff: Certainly. I'll see what I can do. Do you know the course code, by any chance?
[01:11] Woman: Yes. It's JM309.
[01:17] Staff: Great, thank you. That makes it easier for me to find it on the system.
[01:21] Woman: Sure. That's why I made a note of it.
[01:23] Staff: Okay, yes. I've found it here. That's the one on Thursday, isn't it? From 6.30 to 7.45?
[01:30] Woman: That's the one.
[01:32] Staff: Right. It's saying there aren't any places available, I'm afraid. That'll be why you couldn't book a place.
[01:39] Woman: Oh, that's a shame. What other evening courses are there?
[01:43] Staff: There's one called Working with Glass, which is very popular. Course WG891. Does that sound like something that might interest you?
[01:53] Woman: Maybe, but it depends when it is. I'm free every evening during the week, except Tuesday.
[01:59] Staff: Oh, right. That's when it is. From 5.45 until 7. And there are a few places, but I understand that wouldn't be possible for you.
[02:08] Staff: Is that right?
[02:09] Woman: I'm afraid so.
[02:10] Staff: We also run a pottery course, P168. That's every Friday, but it's earlier.
[02:17] Woman: Well, that might work, because I only work until 2 on Fridays.
[02:21] Staff: What time? It starts at 4.15 and runs until 5.30. There's still space if you're interested.
[02:29] Woman: Great. I'll take that place then, please. Can I just ask a couple of questions about the course?
[03:09] Staff: Of course.
[03:10] Woman: So, what will be the date of my first class?
[03:13] Staff: The first day of the term is April the 15th, but your course is on Fridays, so April the 19th will be your first session.
[03:21] Woman: Okay, thank you. I'll make a note of that. And how will I find my class?
[03:26] Staff: You mean, where is it?
[03:27] Woman: Exactly.
[03:29] Staff: You need to go to the Fulwood building. Your class is in there.
[03:32] Woman: Oh. Would you mind spelling that for me?
[03:35] Staff: Sure. F-O-double-L Ward. It's clearly signposted from the college car park.
[03:42] Woman: Oh, speaking of parking, will I be able to use the one at the college?
[03:47] Staff: It's only for students on full-time courses, I'm afraid. And staff, of course.
[03:52] Woman: What about the surgery car park across the road from the college?

[03:56] Staff: That's what I would suggest. They'll be closed by then, and they're happy for their car park to be used. People used to use the library car park next to the college, but we've been asked not to let people park there.
[04:08] Woman: All right. Fair enough. A friend of mine did this course last year, and she said the first thing she produced was a bowl. Do you know if they still do that?
[04:18] Staff: Let me just check. Yes, that's right. In week one. And that's followed by a mug in week two.
[04:28] Woman: Well, let's see how I get on.
[04:31] Staff: Sure. So, if we can sort out the payment next, how would you like to...

passages.title: Prehistoric Park
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Prehistoric Park"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:54] AUDIO: Okay everyone, welcome to Prehistoric Park. Before we go into the park I'd like to give you a few details. Everyone in our group will need to purchase their own tickets and there are reductions available to anyone who's in full-time education. Otherwise it's 22 euros for a full price ticket and that does include senior citizens over the age of 65.

[01:16] AUDIO: No discounts for you I'm afraid but carers, in other words anyone looking after someone with a disability or special need, can also get entry tickets at a lower rate. One of the biggest attractions is the pterodactyl, the roller coaster ride which reaches speeds of 120 kilometers an hour. Now for anyone who's a bit nervous at the prospect of going at that sort of speed I can assure you it's worth it and you'll feel so proud of yourself for being brave when you get off at the end of the ride. In fact a lot of people go straight back on again as quickly as they possibly can.

[01:54] AUDIO: As it's peak season there may be lengthy queues as the day goes on so your best bet may be to have a go on it now before the park fills up. Oh and just so you know they'll only let you onto the ride if you're at least 1 meter 20 tall because obviously safety is a priority. If you need any help once we're in the park do keep an eye open for Prehistoric Park staff. They're the ones wearing the t-shirts or hoodies with a big dinosaur on.

[02:24] AUDIO: They are fantastic at helping you get the most out of your day at the park. For example by suggesting which rides and experiences will be ideal for your group. In case there are any health issues they can arrange for you to speak to a medic and they're also amazing at keeping the kids amused. Real multitaskers these people.

[02:44] AUDIO: One thing you probably won't need them for though is finding your way around because I'll give you all a map but I'll tell you more about that in a few minutes once we've gone into the park. Okay everyone so here we are inside the park. Before you explore the place for yourselves I'll let you know about what there is here and where you can find it. If you open your maps you'll see we are currently at the ticket office.

[03:46] AUDIO: From here it's just a short walk over the bridge to the visitor centre. There you can find more detailed information about the park and of course learn about dinosaurs and the world in which they lived. Connected to the visitor centre is the fossil museum where you can observe several fossils of bones including those brought from the famous local dig. From this room you will also get a splendid panoramic view across the treetop walk over to the biodomes where you can experience a recreation of the mesozoic era the age of the dinosaurs.

[04:21] AUDIO: Returning to the visitor centre there are various routes to take around the park. The first leads from the visitor centre towards the northwest part of the park in which you can find attractions for younger visitors before reaching the pterodactyl roller coaster. But on the way to this you will first pass the adventure playground on the left and the excavation pit which was the original inspiration for the park on the right. The second path leads directly from the visitor centre to the biodomes and the next two routes both head from the building containing the visitor centre towards the river that runs along the southern edge of the park and you'll find the cafe at the point where these two paths connect just to the north of the stream.

[05:03] AUDIO: You can take paths from the biodomes and the central area of the park over to the riverside walk in the very east of the park. Here boardwalks and bridges weave over a network of streams and lead to a car park via the gift shop. Before you get there you'll come across a small island with a tranquil picnic site and I must say the weather looks perfect for a picnic today.
